Tested with CPython 3.14.10 (both the default and the 3.14t free-threaded builds) installed through uv 0.13.9, on an 8-core Linux x86-64 machine. The commands and outputs below are from that machine. We could not build a Docker image there, so the container section is based on the same uv commands plus the official image tag list.

What "free threaded" means in Python 3.14

A normal CPython build has a global interpreter lock (GIL): only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound threads do not speed up. The free-threaded build removes that lock. Threads run in parallel on separate cores, at the cost of a different ABI, extra memory use and a small single-thread slowdown.

The official Python docs describe it plainly: free-threaded execution allows full use of available processing power, "while not all software will benefit from this automatically", and some third-party packages with extension modules "will re-enable the GIL". On the pyperformance suite the docs put the average single-threaded overhead between about 1% on macOS aarch64 and 8% on x86-64 Linux.

It is a separate interpreter, not a flag on the normal one. The binary is called python3.14t. A wheel built for the normal interpreter (cp314) will not load there; it needs a cp314t build.

Install Python 3.14 free threaded with uv

uv knows the t suffix:

uv python install 3.14t
uv run --python 3.14t python -VV
uv venv --python 3.14t .venv

python -VV prints "free-threading build" in the version string. To check the GIL state in a running process, use the function the docs recommend:

import sys, sysconfig
print(sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED"))  # 1 on a free-threaded build
print(sys._is_gil_enabled())                         # False when the GIL is off

The two answers differ on purpose. The config variable tells you what the build can do. sys._is_gil_enabled() tells you what the process is doing right now. On our box:

3.14.10  Py_GIL_DISABLED = 0  gil enabled = True     (default build)
3.14.10  Py_GIL_DISABLED = 1  gil enabled = False    (3.14t)
3.14.10  Py_GIL_DISABLED = 1  gil enabled = True     (3.14t with PYTHON_GIL=1)

You can force the lock back on with the PYTHON_GIL=1 environment variable or -X gil=1, and off with 0. We confirmed python -X gil=1 reports the GIL as enabled.

Python 3.14 free threaded benchmark

The test is deliberately simple: a recursive fib(32) in N threads, with N from 1 to 4, timed with time.perf_counter().

import threading, time

def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

def run(nthreads, n=32):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=fib, args=(n,)) for _ in range(nthreads)]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
    return time.perf_counter() - start

Results (the free-threaded numbers are from two runs, which agreed within noise):

Build 1 thread 2 threads 4 threads Throughput vs serial at 4 threads
3.14 (GIL) 0.15 s 0.30 s 0.60 s 1.0x
3.14t (GIL off) 0.15 s 0.15 s 0.15 to 0.16 s 3.6x to 3.9x
3.14t, PYTHON_GIL=1 0.15 s 0.30 s 0.62 s 1.0x

Four threads on the normal build take four times as long as one, because they queue on the lock. On 3.14t they all finish in about the time of one. Setting PYTHON_GIL=1 on the free-threaded interpreter brought the old behaviour straight back, which is a handy way to A/B test your own code.

Single-thread speed was the same to two decimal places in this one benchmark. Do not read that as "no overhead": the docs' 1% to 8% average is across many workloads, and a different benchmark will show a gap.

Not everything scales

We also ran a thread pool hashing 8 buffers with hashlib.sha256 (300,000 rounds each, 64-byte inputs):

3.14   1 / 4 / 8 workers: 0.56 s / 0.57 s / 0.54 s
3.14t  1 / 4 / 8 workers: 0.62 s / 0.84 s / 0.87 s

Neither build scaled, and the free-threaded one was slower with more workers. We did not dig into why, and we are not claiming a cause. The lesson is practical: measure the real workload. A pure-Python loop scaled almost linearly, a workload dominated by one C library call did not.

The race condition you meet only without the GIL

On the normal build, count += 1 from several threads usually looks fine, because a thread rarely gets switched out in the middle of the operation. Without the GIL it is a real race. We ran four threads that each did two million increments of a shared global:

3.14   gil_enabled=True   expected 8000000, got 8000000
3.14t  gil_enabled=False  expected 8000000, got 2238627, lost 5761373
3.14t  gil_enabled=False  expected 8000000, got 2248157, lost 5751843

The same code with threading.Lock around the increment returned the exact total on both builds (800,000 of 800,000 with fewer iterations). The Python docs say the same thing in softer words: built-in types such as dict, list and set have internal locks, but you should use threading.Lock or other synchronization primitives "instead of relying on the internal locks of built-in types, when possible."

If your code only worked because the GIL hid a race, free threading will expose it. Run your tests on 3.14t before you ship it.

Which packages re-enable the GIL

Import a C extension that has not declared free-threading support and Python turns the GIL back on for the whole process, with a warning. We built a tiny extension without the Py_mod_gil slot to see exactly what happens:

RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load module 'legacyext',
which has not declared that it can run safely without the GIL. To override this behavior and keep
the GIL disabled (at your own risk), run with PYTHON_GIL=0 or -Xgil=0.
before: False
after okext: False        (module that declares Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED)
after legacyext: True

Setting PYTHON_GIL=0 kept it off after the same import, which can crash if the module is really not thread-safe, so treat it as a debugging tool and not a fix.

For real packages, we created a 3.14t venv and installed with --only-binary :all: so uv would not compile anything:

Package Result on 3.14t today
numpy 2.5.5 installs, GIL stays off after import
pydantic 2.14.4 (pydantic-core 2.50.5) installs, GIL stays off
fastapi 0.165.0, uvicorn 0.54.0 install, GIL stays off
httptools 0.9.0, uvloop 0.23.0 install, GIL stays off
orjson no binary wheel found; uv could not resolve one, and a source build failed on our box because it needs a Rust toolchain
psycopg[binary] no binary wheel found

That is a snapshot from 28 November 2026 on Linux x86-64, not a promise. Two trackers keep the live picture: py-free-threading.github.io/tracking and hugovk.github.io/free-threaded-wheels. The most useful check is the cheapest one: import every dependency in a fresh 3.14t venv and print sys._is_gil_enabled() afterwards.

Docker and Python 3.14 free threaded

There is no official free-threaded tag in the Docker library. The official Python image lists 3.14-slim-trixie, 3.14-trixie, 3.14-alpine and the other normal variants, but no 3.14t. A request for 3.13t and 3.14t images is still open as docker-library/python issue 1082. So FROM python:3.14-slim gives you the GIL build, and setting PYTHON_GIL=0 on it does not help: the default interpreter aborts at startup with Fatal Python error: config_read_gil: Disabling the GIL is not supported by this build, which is what we got on 3.14.10.

Instead, install the interpreter with uv in your own image. This is the same flow as our FastAPI Dockerfile with uv:

FROM debian:trixie-slim
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest /uv /uvx /bin/
ENV UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR=/opt/python
WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN uv sync --frozen --no-dev --python 3.14t
COPY . .
CMD ["uv", "run", "--no-sync", "--python", "3.14t", "python", "-m", "app"]

We did not build this exact image because the box has no Docker daemon access, but we ran the same uv lock, uv sync --frozen --no-dev --python 3.14t and uv run --no-sync --python 3.14t python -m app steps on a small project that depends on fastapi and uvicorn, and the app printed gil enabled: False. Check your own build once. For a workspace with several packages, the uv workspace guide shows how to sync one member. A startup check is worth adding to the app itself:

import sys
assert not sys._is_gil_enabled(), "GIL got re-enabled by an import"

Put it after your imports in the entry point, so a dependency that silently re-enables the lock fails the deploy instead of the benchmark. In a FastAPI app the lifespan hook is a natural place for it.

When free threading is worth it

Good fits: CPU-bound pure-Python work you currently split across processes (shared memory without pickling), thread pools doing parsing or transformation, and numerical code that calls into already-supported libraries from many threads.

Poor fits: I/O-bound services. Threads waiting on a network call already release the GIL, so asyncio or normal threads were fine before. If your app mostly calls a model endpoint, as in our Docker Compose models guide, free threading will not make those calls faster. It also changes memory use: the docs warn that all interned strings become immortal, None takes 32 bytes instead of 16 on x86-64, and freed memory can be returned later because of deferred reclamation.

A sensible rollout: run your test suite on 3.14t in CI next to the normal build, add the GIL assertion, fix the locks it exposes, and only then benchmark production-shaped load.

FAQ

How do I install Python 3.14 free threaded?

With uv: uv python install 3.14t, then uv run --python 3.14t python -VV or uv venv --python 3.14t. On macOS and Windows the official installers have an optional free-threaded build, and the binary is named python3.14t.

How do I check whether the GIL is disabled?

Call sys._is_gil_enabled(). It returns False when the GIL is off. sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") only tells you the build supports it.

Why did the GIL turn back on after an import?

A C extension did not declare that it can run without the GIL, so Python enabled the lock for the whole process and printed a RuntimeWarning. Update the package, find a free-threaded wheel, or avoid it. PYTHON_GIL=0 forces it off but is unsafe for modules that are not thread-safe.

Is there a free-threaded official Docker image?

Not at the time of writing. The official Python image has no 3.14t tag and the request is still open. Install 3.14t with uv in your own image.

Is free-threaded Python faster?

For CPU-bound threaded code, yes: our 4-thread test finished in the time of one on 3.14t and four times as long on the normal build. Single-threaded code can be slightly slower, and some workloads, like our hashing test, did not scale at all.

title: CSV Clean X: Robust Python CSV Pipelines
summary:
CSV Clean X: A Robust Python Library for CSV Pipelines

When working with data pipelines in Python, cleaning and standardizing CSV data is a common bottleneck. Today, we're introducing CSV Clean X, a lightweight and robust Python library designed to streamline data cleaning, whitespace stripping, missing value handling, and duplicate removal.

Features

  • Whitespace Stripping: Automatically cleans leading and trailing whitespaces from string fields.
  • Missing Value Handling: Option to drop rows with missing or empty values.
  • Duplicate Removal: Ensures unique dataset rows effortlessly.
  • Lightweight & Fast: Zero heavy dependencies, pure Python implementation with robust unit testing.

Installation & Usage

You can find the project repository on GitHub: qtnt2xxx-wq/csv-clean-x.

from csv_clean_x.pipeline import CsvCleanPipeline

data = [
    {"name": " Alice ", "age": "30"},
    {"name": "Bob", "age": "25"},
    {"name": " Alice ", "age": "30"}
]

pipeline = CsvCleanPipeline(data)
cleaned_data = pipeline.run(strip=True, drop_missing=False)
print(cleaned_data)

Check out the repo and contribute!

title: VAP evidence packs in Python: why the caller must pin the scope
summary:
By 上村十勝 (Tokachi Kamimura).

A collection of signed AI records can be internally consistent and still fail the review you intended to perform. One reason is that the submitter may have changed what counts as a complete collection.

This tutorial uses the experimental vap-interop-demo/0.2.0 package in the VAP repository to reproduce that distinction. First, run eight committed fixtures. Then keep a reduced, re-signed pack unchanged and change only the verifier's scope pin: the result changes from FAIL to PASS.

That is a demonstration of the trust-input boundary. It is not a signature forgery, a production exploit, or a VAP conformance test.

日本語概要：上村十勝が、VAPリポジトリの実験用検証器を使い、署名・監査対象の範囲・記録の欠落を切り分けます。掲載結果は合成データによるローカル実験です。

What is being verified?

VAP — Verifiable AI Provenance Framework defines requirements for reviewing recorded AI decisions after the fact. The framework specification is v1.2.0 Draft 3 at the source revision used here.

The interoperability demo is a separate, first-party experimental contract. Its flat events and demo receipts are not the framework's abstract event and AnchorRecord formats. Its attempt/outcome rule is a local scenario choice, not a universal VAP completeness requirement.

The primary fixture describes two fictional attempts:

  • One records DENIED_AUTOMATION and requests human review.
  • One records APPROVED.

Both belong in the valid pack. A verification PASS means that the submitted evidence satisfies the demo contract; it does not mean that every action was approved or that a real action occurred.

The seven checks behind PASS

The Python verifier reports these checks on success:

Check Question answered within this demo
contract-and-shape Do the inputs use the supported contract, exact fields and restricted JSON values?
pinned-scope Does the scope digest match the separately supplied trust configuration?
event-signatures Do event hashes and signatures verify under the configured producer key?
sequence-and-scope Are IDs unique, sequence numbers contiguous, and supplied chain, policy and times within scope?
rfc6962-root Does the recomputed Merkle root match the submitted root?
role-receipts Do the configured producer, observer and anchor records bind the same root, scope and count?
attempt-outcome-bijection Does each declared attempt have one later outcome, with the expected number of distinct attempts?

The serialization contract is DEMO-ASCII-SAFEINT-JSON-v1: printable ASCII strings and bounded integers, with duplicate keys and floating-point number tokens rejected. It is not support for the entire RFC 8785 input domain. The six-event positive fixture also exercises an RFC 6962 tree whose leaf count is not a power of two.

Reproduce the fixed fixtures

Use a new directory for the checkout:

git clone https://github.com/veritaschain/vap-spec.git vap-scope-demo
cd vap-scope-demo
git checkout --detach 2a18ae7c77a4afcb7468345db2424076530c7630
cd interop/vap-evidence-pack-demo

python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

The local run reported here used macOS 27.2.1, Python 3.14.3 and cryptography 50.0.2 on 28 November 2026. Upstream documents Python 3.12 and Node.js 24; this article reports a Python-only run with the stated Python-version difference.

Save the following as check_article.py beside verify_python.py. It verifies the ten fixture/trust files against the committed manifest before running the eight cases. It also distinguishes a missing file from rejected evidence.

import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
vectors = root / "test-vectors"
manifest = json.loads((vectors / "manifest.json").read_text())
for name, expected in manifest["files"].items():
    data = (vectors / name).read_bytes()
    if len(data) != expected["bytes"] or hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() != expected["sha256"]:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Fixture bytes changed: {name}")

results = []
def run(pack, trust, expected_verdict, expected_exit, label):
    proc = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, str(root / "verify_python.py"), str(pack),
         "--trust", str(trust), "--json"],
        text=True, capture_output=True, check=False)
    try:
        report = json.loads(proc.stdout)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{label}: verifier did not return JSON; exit={proc.returncode}, stderr={proc.stderr}") from exc
    if proc.returncode != expected_exit or report.get("verdict") != expected_verdict:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{label}: unexpected result: {proc.returncode}, {report}")
    results.append({"case": label, "exit": proc.returncode, **report})
    print(f"{label}: {report['verdict']} / exit {proc.returncode}")

for case in manifest["vectors"]:
    run(vectors / case["pack"], vectors / case["trust"],
        case["expected_verdict"], case["expected_exit_code"], case["pack"])

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="vap-scope-test-") as directory:
    temp = Path(directory)
    run(temp / "does-not-exist.json", vectors / "demo-trust.json",
        "ERROR", 2, "missing file")
    pack = json.loads((vectors / "invalid-rebound-scope.json").read_text())
    trust = json.loads((vectors / "demo-trust.json").read_text())
    # Deliberately unsafe: this demonstrates why the caller must authenticate trust input.
    trust["scope_commitment"] = pack["scope_commitment"]
    substituted = temp / "substituted-trust.json"
    substituted.write_text(json.dumps(trust), encoding="utf-8")
    run(vectors / "invalid-rebound-scope.json", vectors / "demo-trust.json",
        "FAIL", 1, "rebound scope / original trust")
    run(vectors / "invalid-rebound-scope.json", substituted,
        "PASS", 0, "rebound scope / substituted trust")

(root / "observed-results.json").write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=2)+"\n")

Run it:

python check_article.py

Observed output:

valid-pack.json: PASS / exit 0
valid-six-events.json: PASS / exit 0
invalid-tampered-event.json: FAIL / exit 1
invalid-omitted-outcome.json: FAIL / exit 1
invalid-split-view.json: FAIL / exit 1
invalid-omitted-pair.json: FAIL / exit 1
invalid-rebound-scope.json: FAIL / exit 1
invalid-untrusted-signer.json: FAIL / exit 1
missing file: ERROR / exit 2
rebound scope / original trust: FAIL / exit 1
rebound scope / substituted trust: PASS / exit 0

The script writes the complete verifier reports, including error messages, to observed-results.json. Fixture bytes were checked against the manifest, and the retrieved source files were checked against their Git blob IDs at the pinned commit.

The manifest's SHA-256 in this run was:

bc05d2de41f713b8a19110bcfde864b44e2beaccebf3108d59a0611750262953

A digest fixes the bytes being discussed. It does not, by itself, authenticate whoever supplied those bytes.

Why the scope substitution passes

The invalid-rebound-scope.json fixture reduces the submitted collection and changes the declaration to fit it. The fixture generator rebuilds and re-signs that collection with the public test keys.

With the original trust file, the verifier rejects it:

scope does not match the caller's pinned commitment

The final experiment deliberately copies the pack's scope_commitment into a temporary trust file. The keys stay unchanged, and the pack stays unchanged. The verifier now accepts the pack relative to the replacement declaration.

Do not derive the trusted scope from the pack in an actual integration. This line is deliberately unsafe:

trust["scope_commitment"] = pack["scope_commitment"]

It turns a caller-selected expectation into a value chosen by the submitter. Passing all later signature, root and pairing checks cannot repair that loss.

The separate file boundary alone is also insufficient: an integration must establish why its selected trust configuration is acceptable, who can change it, and how the expected scope was determined. This demo does not implement that approval process or prove that a declaration existed before the recorded events.

Omission checks answer different questions

The two omission fixtures are useful because the remaining collection is rebuilt and re-signed:

  • Missing outcome: an attempt remains without the one later outcome required by this scenario.
  • Missing pair: the remaining attempts each have outcomes, but there are fewer distinct attempts than the pinned declaration expects.

An application that checks only surviving signatures misses both kinds of inconsistency. An application that checks only matching attempt/outcome IDs misses the second.

The expected count is still an input assumption. Neither fixture establishes an inventory of all real activity. An action that no available record implies cannot be recovered from this dataset.

Keep rejection separate from an operational error

For this CLI, the contract distinguishes:

Result Exit Meaning
PASS 0 All checks for this experimental contract succeeded
FAIL 1 Pack or trust input violates the contract
ERROR 2 Usage or file access prevented evaluation

A negative test must require FAIL and exit 1. Treating every nonzero exit as a successful rejection would let a missing fixture pass the test. The harness checks both values.

Argument-parsing errors, such as omitting --trust, exit 2 before a JSON report is produced. The harness therefore treats missing or invalid JSON as an execution problem, not as a detected evidence defect.

What this run does not establish

All three demo private keys are public. The observer and anchor are simulated roles, and DEMO_ANCHOR_RECEIPT is a signed fixture, not a receipt from an external service. Supplied timestamps are checked for consistency; they do not provide trusted time.

These results demonstrate behavior of the unmodified reference verifier on named synthetic inputs. They do not establish real-world signer identity, independent observation, production anchoring, complete capture, VAP/profile conformance, or the correctness of an AI decision. No Node.js execution or full upstream test-suite run is claimed here.

The framework's anchor-granularity omission boundary is discussed separately in VAP v1.2 §4.1.7 and §11.1. The demo's pairing rule must not be presented as proof of those framework requirements.

Author and preparation

上村十勝 (Tokachi Kamimura) is the founder of VSO and Representative Director of VeritasChain Co., Ltd., which operates VSO. This is an affiliated, first-party demonstration using published reference code, not an independent validation. Official author profile.

This article and its test harness were prepared by an AI assistant. The assistant checked the cited source revision and executed the reported local tests; no independent human review is claimed.

    # Deliberately unsafe: this demonstrates why the caller must authenticate trust input.
    trust["scope_commitment"] = pack["scope_commitment"]
    substituted = temp / "substituted-trust.json"
    substituted.write_text(json.dumps(trust), encoding="utf-8")
    run(vectors / "invalid-rebound-scope.json", vectors / "demo-trust.json",
        "FAIL", 1, "rebound scope / original trust")

The script writes the complete verifier reports, including error messages, to observed-results.json. Fixture bytes were checked against the manifest, and the retrieved source files were checked against their Git blob IDs at the pinned commit.

The manifest's SHA-256 in this run was:

bc05d2de41f713b8a19110bcfde864b44e2beaccebf3108d59a0611750262953

A digest fixes the bytes being discussed. It does not, by itself, authenticate whoever supplied those bytes.

Why the scope substitution passes

The invalid-rebound-scope.json fixture reduces the submitted collection and changes the declaration to fit it. The fixture generator rebuilds and re-signs that collection with the public test keys.

With the original trust file, the verifier rejects it:

scope does not match the caller's pinned commitment

The final experiment deliberately copies the pack's scope_commitment into a temporary trust file. The keys stay unchanged, and the pack stays unchanged. The verifier now accepts the pack relative to the replacement declaration.

Do not derive the trusted scope from the pack in an actual integration. This line is deliberately unsafe:

trust["scope_commitment"] = pack["scope_commitment"]

It turns a caller-selected expectation into a value chosen by the submitter. Passing all later signature, root and pairing checks cannot repair that loss.

The separate file boundary alone is also insufficient: an integration must establish why its selected trust configuration is acceptable, who can change it, and how the expected scope was determined. This demo does not implement that approval process or prove that a declaration existed before the recorded events.

Omission checks answer different questions

The two omission fixtures are useful because the remaining collection is rebuilt and re-signed:

  • Missing outcome: an attempt remains without the one later outcome required by this scenario.
  • Missing pair: the remaining attempts each have outcomes, but there are fewer distinct attempts than the pinned declaration expects.

An application that checks only surviving signatures misses both kinds of inconsistency. An application that checks only matching attempt/outcome IDs misses the second.

The expected count is still an input assumption. Neither fixture establishes an inventory of all real activity. An action that no available record implies cannot be recovered from this dataset.

Keep rejection separate from an operational error

For this CLI, the contract distinguishes:

Result Exit Meaning
PASS 0 All checks for this experimental contract succeeded
FAIL 1 Pack or trust input violates the contract
ERROR 2 Usage or file access prevented evaluation

A negative test must require FAIL and exit 1. Treating every nonzero exit as a successful rejection would let a missing fixture pass the test. The harness checks both values.

Argument-parsing errors, such as omitting --trust, exit 2 before a JSON report is produced. The harness therefore treats missing or invalid JSON as an execution problem, not as a detected evidence defect.

What this run does not establish

All three demo private keys are public. The observer and anchor are simulated roles, and DEMO_ANCHOR_RECEIPT is a signed fixture, not a receipt from an external service. Supplied timestamps are checked for consistency; they do not provide trusted time.

These results demonstrate behavior of the unmodified reference verifier on named synthetic inputs. They do not establish real-world signer identity, independent observation, production anchoring, complete capture, VAP/profile conformance, or the correctness of an AI decision. No Node.js execution or full upstream test-suite run is claimed here.

The framework's anchor-granularity omission boundary is discussed separately in VAP v1.2 §4.1.7 and §11.1. The demo's pairing rule must not be presented as proof of those framework requirements.

title: Auditing Documents & Images with Gemini Decisions API
summary:
Check any PDF, draft, or image against 1,000 criteria at once—with zero output tokens

Introduction

In my previous article, "Zero-Output-Token AI in Google Apps Script with Gemini Decisions API" Ref (source repository Ref), I demonstrated how Google DeepMind's Gemini Decisions API (POST https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/decisions, powered by gemini-decision-1) Ref fits Google Workspace automation—covering Gmail inbox labeling, model cascade routing, and a Google Sheets PDF compliance audit. Among those examples, the PDF compliance audit drew an especially strong response, and I received inquiries about it from readers across many different fields.

The origin of that idea was actually very personal: before turning it into a Google Sheets demo, I had been using the Decisions API in my own daily writing workflow to check my own research papers, technical articles, manuscripts, and drafts against a self-defined set of review criteria all at once, surfacing issues instantaneously. When developers first encounter a classification endpoint like the Decisions API, the natural mental model is "Many-Inputs × Few-Labels"—classifying a stream of emails or support tickets into three to five categories. Flipping that geometry to "1-Input × up to 1,000-Criteria"—sending one rich multimodal artifact (a PDF, research paper, article manuscript, or ad creative) once and evaluating it against up to 1,000 independent questions in a single forward pass—turned out to be a usage pattern that most users had never envisioned.

Because of that response, I decided to write this dedicated follow-up article focused exclusively on this technique, which I refer to as Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA). Because gemini-decision-1 evaluates all questions against the shared input simultaneously without autoregressive text decoding Ref, ZOMA produces strictly zero output tokens ($0.00 output cost, with input tokens billed once at $0.10 per 1M input tokens) Ref while returning calibrated probabilities (0.01 to 0.99), discrete choices, and ordinal rubric scores (0–4). Moving beyond Google Apps Script into a universal, dependency-light Python 3 CLI published at gemini-decisions-api-python Ref, this article presents a reusable ZOMA auditing and weighted-scoring architecture and validates it across five live multimodal use cases (83 total criteria across Markdown, PDF, and PNG inputs). While I designed the core scenario and evaluation criteria for each of the five use cases myself, the sample input documents used to demonstrate and reproduce each run were generated with Gemini via samples/generate_samples.py Ref so that anyone can reproduce every benchmark without proprietary files; every latency, token count, probability, score, and cost figure reported in this article comes directly from live API runs, and you can immediately swap in your own local files and custom checklists.

In Plain English: What Is ZOMA?

Imagine handing a 20-page vendor contract, a research manuscript draft, an advertising banner, a student essay, or a grant proposal to a meticulous reviewer along with a structured checklist—and receiving every checkbox verdict, every 0–4 quality rating, and a clear flag on any ambiguous clause that needs human judgment back in under one second, for a fraction of a cent. That is Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA). Instead of asking an AI chatbot to write long prose explanations one question at a time, ZOMA sends your document once, evaluates dozens or hundreds of independent checklist rules simultaneously, and lets deterministic Python code handle all final math and pass/fail decisions.

Key Terms in Plain English

  • Single Forward Pass & Zero Output Tokens: Standard AI chatbots generate answers one word (token) at a time, which adds latency and output billing. A single forward pass reads your document once and returns structured numeric answers directly, generating zero written text and zero output-token cost.
  • Calibrated Probability (0.01–0.99): A reliability-tuned percentage expressed from 0.01 (1% likely "Yes") to 0.99 (99% likely "Yes"). When the model is genuinely unsure (for example, 0.72), the score sits in the middle instead of pretending to be 99% certain.
  • Question Types (noul, choice, score): The three structured question formats supported by the Decisions API—noul for Yes/No checks, choice for picking one label from a fixed list, and score for rating quality on an ordered rubric such as 0 to 4.
  • OCR-Free Multimodal Input: Sending PDFs and images (like PNG banners) directly to the AI model as-is, without running a separate Optical Character Recognition (OCR) or PDF-to-text converter first.
  • CLI, JSON/YAML & Dry-Run: A Command-Line Interface (CLI) is a lightweight terminal program; JSON and YAML are plain-text formats used to write your checklist rules; and --dry-run checks your files and rules locally before making any paid API call.
  • Knock-Out Gate: A mandatory eligibility requirement (such as a maximum grant budget cap) where failing that single rule disqualifies a submission immediately, regardless of how high its overall quality score is.

1. Why Gemini Decisions API Excels at ZOMA & Architecture

Low latency and low cost are the most immediately visible advantages of gemini-decision-1, yet its deeper architectural strengths are what make Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA) production-grade across legal, editorial, visual, and academic domains Ref:

  • Sub-Second Single Forward-Pass Latency: Because the model evaluates all questions in a single prefill forward pass (reading the document once without generating text word-by-word) without autoregressive token-by-token decoding, end-to-end latency remains flat and sub-second (497.4–856.4 ms live measured across 14–20 criteria) instead of scaling linearly with output length.
  • Ultra-Low Cost with Strictly Zero Output Tokens: Shared document input tokens are billed once at $0.10 per 1M input tokens Ref, while output and thinking tokens remain strictly 0 ($0.00 output cost), cutting input volume by over 92% compared to sequential per-criterion calls.
  • Mathematically Calibrated Probabilities & Native Confidence Gating: Unlike generative LLMs whose self-reported verbal confidence is often poorly calibrated, gemini-decision-1 returns statistically calibrated probabilities (0.01–0.99) and confidence scores, enabling reliable automated NEEDS_REVIEW escalation thresholds (such as 0.85).
  • Zero JSON Parse Failures & Closed-Set Schema Guarantees: Because no free-form text is decoded into JSON strings, malformed JSON, hallucinated enum values, and schema drift are structurally impossible across noul, choice (2–255 options), and score (2–255 ordered rubric tiers) primitives Ref.
  • High-Density Parallel Batching (Up to 1,000 Independent Questions): A single request evaluates up to 1,000 independent criteria against the exact same shared context without cross-question prompt contamination or attention degradation from massive compound instructions.
  • 262,144-Token Unified Multimodal Context (OCR-Free): A single shared input accepts up to 262,144 tokens (256K) across mixed modalities—text, JSON, PDFs, images, audio, and video Ref—allowing native inspection of multi-page PDFs and high-resolution ad creatives without external OCR or PDF-to-text pipelines.
  • High Reproducibility for Programmatic Control Flow: Without autoregressive sampling drift or variable thinking-token traces, probability outputs remain highly repeatable across runs, making gemini-decision-1 a dependable upstream signal provider for deterministic downstream software logic.

Separation of Concerns

A common problem in LLM-based evaluation pipelines is asking a single generative model to read a document, judge 20 criteria, apply custom business weights, check hard eligibility rules, and sum the final score in one autoregressive JSON response. When AI judgment and arithmetic are mixed together, models exhibit silent summation drift, inconsistent threshold enforcement, and brittle JSON formatting errors.

To prevent these problems by design, our Python CLI enforces a strict two-layer separation of concerns, illustrated in Figure 1.


Figure 1: Shifting from sequential autoregressive LLM loops to 1-Input × up to 1,000-Criteria evaluation with strict separation between gemini-decision-1 inference (client.py) and deterministic Python aggregation (evaluator.py).

As shown in Figure 1, the pipeline divides responsibility across three focused modules:

  • Stateless Multimodal Transport (cli/client.py) Ref: Reads a local .md, .txt, .pdf, .png, .jpg, .jpeg, or .webp file once, Base64-encodes binary documents and images natively without OCR middleware (packaging PDFs and images directly for the API without separate text-extraction tools), authenticates strictly via the x-goog-api-key HTTP header, automatically chunks checklists exceeding 1,000 questions into compliant batches, applies bounded exponential backoff on HTTP 429/5xx, and normalizes proto-JSON response fields into typed Python dictionaries.
  • Zero-Output-Token Semantic Inference (gemini-decision-1): Evaluates every criterion independently against the shared input in one forward pass, returning calibrated noul probabilities (0.01–0.99), choice probability distributions, or score expected values and ordinal bucket distributions—with 0 output tokens generated.
  • Deterministic Evaluation Engine (cli/evaluator.py) Ref: Operates completely offline with zero network I/O. It applies exact threshold rules, risk-flag inversions (expected: "no"), hard knock-out gates, weighted linear scaling, negative penalty deductions, and borderline/low-confidence escalation in pure Python—verified offline by the Stage-3 boundary stress test suite (an automated offline check that verifies the math handles edge cases like zero scores or borderline ties) cli/test_evaluator_stress.py Ref.

This decoupling guarantees that LLM arithmetic hallucination is structurally impossible: the AI model only produces calibrated per-criterion signals, while Python owns every threshold comparison, weighted sum, and pass/fail verdict. Table 1 compares the two deterministic operating modes built into evaluator.py alongside a traditional autoregressive LLM loop.


Table 1: Comparison of Naive Autoregressive LLM Loops vs. Gemini Decisions API Mode A (audit) and Mode B (weighted_scoring) across token scaling, output tokens, arithmetic determinism, and human-in-the-loop gating.

Table 1 highlights why a single checklist schema can drive two distinct enterprise patterns:

  • Mode A (audit): Designed for binary compliance, pre-flight linting, and risk scanning. Each noul criterion specifies expected: "yes" (required safeguard) or expected: "no" (prohibited risk flag). Any signal whose confidence falls below confidence_threshold (default 0.85, i.e., 0.15 < P < 0.85) is routed automatically to NEEDS_REVIEW rather than guessed. For choice criteria, explicit fail_choices or review_choices trigger FAIL or NEEDS_REVIEW; for score criteria, expected scores are gated against pass_min and fail_max.
  • Mode B (weighted_scoring): Designed for rubric grading, grant screening, and procurement scoring. Criteria can be marked as knockout: true (hard eligibility gates where a FAIL immediately disqualifies the submission regardless of points, and low confidence forces NEEDS_REVIEW), positive-weight noul or score dimensions (where an ordinal 0–4 score contributes (score / max_scale) * weight points), or negative-weight noul penalty flags. If the final total falls within ±borderline_margin of cutoff_score, or if too many items exhibit low confidence (max_low_conf_for_auto), the engine escalates the overall verdict to NEEDS_REVIEW.

Mode A & Mode B End-to-End Workflows

Before diving into CLI commands and live numbers, Figure 2 and Figure 3 map the five end-to-end workflows we evaluated across both operating modes.


Figure 2: End-to-end Mode A (audit) pipelines for UC1 (Markdown Manuscript Linter), UC2 (Multi-Page Vendor Contract PDF Risk Scanner), and UC3 (High-Resolution Ad Creative PNG QA), each executed in a single API batch.


Figure 3: Mode B (weighted_scoring) execution pipelines for UC4 (Cybersecurity Essay Rubric Grading) and UC5 (R&D Grant Proposal Knock-Out + Weighted Screening), where Python deterministically computes final totals and cutoff gates.

2. Quickstart & Reusable Python CLI Usage

All scripts, sample inputs, checklists, and saved live results are published in tanaikech/gemini-decisions-api-python Ref. The CLI requires only Python 3, requests, and PyYAML (requirements.txt Ref). Clone the repository, install dependencies, and export your Gemini API key once (the client sends the key solely in the x-goog-api-key header and never embeds it in URLs):

3. Mode A Live Walkthrough & Empirical Results

Mode A (audit) targets high-precision defect detection across text, multi-page PDFs, and raw visual creatives. Following the three single-batch pipelines mapped in Figure 2, we examine each Mode A use case individually alongside its dedicated live test results infographic (Figure 4, Figure 5, and Figure 6).

How to read the live numbers in Sections 3 and 4:

  • Required checks (expected: "yes"): We want the document to contain this element, so a high probability (p >= 0.85) means PASS, while a very low probability (p <= 0.15) means FAIL (missing requirement).
  • Risk & defect flags (expected: "no"): We want this problem to be absent, so a low probability (p <= 0.15) means PASS (safe), while a high probability (p >= 0.85) means FAIL (risk or violation detected).
  • Human-review zone (0.15 < P < 0.85): Whenever the model's confidence is below 0.85, the tool refuses to guess and routes that criterion to NEEDS_REVIEW for a human reviewer.
  • Rubric scores (0–4, e.g., 3.17 / 4): Rather than forcing a blunt whole number, the model returns a probability distribution across levels 0 through 4 and computes the weighted average (expected score) for fine-grained grading.

Use Case 1: Manuscript & Technical Document Semantic Linter (uc1_manuscript_draft.md)

Use Case 3: Ad Creative OCR-Free Multimodal QA (uc3_ad_creative.png)

4. Mode B Live Walkthrough & Empirical Results

Mode B (weighted_scoring) moves beyond pass/fail checklists into quantitative rubric grading and multi-stage eligibility screening. Following the deterministic aggregation and knock-out pipelines illustrated in Figure 3, we walk through each Mode B live evaluation with its dedicated scoring breakdown infographic (Figure 7 and Figure 8).

Use Case 4: Cybersecurity Case Study Weighted Rubric Grading (uc4_student_essay.pdf)

In Use Case 4, a 52,224-byte student cybersecurity case study PDF (samples/uc4_student_essay.pdf Ref) was graded against a 100-point rubric (samples/uc4_checklist.json Ref; saved output: results/uc4_result.json Ref) containing 14 criteria: 6 mandatory element checks worth +5.0 pts each (30.0 pts), 4 ordinal 0–4 rubric dimensions totaling 70.0 pts, and 4 negative penalty flags (-10.0 to -15.0 pts), with a 75.0 cutoff and ±3.0 borderline margin. The single Decisions API call finished in 702.58 ms (0 retries) using 3,261 input tokens (2,221 text + 1,040 image tokens) and 0 output tokens (estimated cost $0.000326), saving 13 sequential API calls. The deterministic final score was 86.17 / 100.0 (86.2%), yielding PASS, as detailed in Figure 7.

Because every noul item exceeded 0.85 confidence and every score item concentrated its top-2 adjacent probability mass (P(3) + P(4) = 0.920–0.958) above 0.85, low_confidence_items was empty (0 / 2 cap), enabling safe automated grading.

In Use Case 5, a 60,088-byte R&D grant proposal PDF (samples/uc5_grant_proposal.pdf Ref) was screened against 15 criteria (samples/uc5_checklist.json Ref; saved output: results/uc5_result.json Ref): 4 hard knock-out eligibility gates (weight = 0.0, mandatory pass), 6 completeness/impact binary checks (+5.0 pts each = 30.0 pts), 4 ordinal merit rubric scores (70.0 pts total), and 1 conflict-of-interest / ethics penalty flag (-15.0 pts), against a 70.0 cutoff and ±3.0 borderline margin. The single API call completed in 769.60 ms (0 retries) using 3,339 input tokens (2,299 text + 1,040 image tokens) and 0 output tokens (estimated cost $0.000334), saving 14 sequential API calls. The proposal cleared all 4 knock-out gates and scored 91.40 / 100.0 (91.4%), returning PASS, as presented in Figure 8.


Figure 8: Live Mode B screening results for UC5 (uc5_grant_proposal.pdf, 15 criteria, 769.6 ms, 3,339 input tokens, 0 output tokens, $0.000334), verifying 4/4 hard knock-out eligibility gates, 30.0/30.0 completeness points, 61.40/70.0 merit points, and 91.40/100.0 total score vs. the 70.0 cutoff.

In evaluator.py, if any single knock-out gate had returned FAIL, the overall verdict would have been forced to FAIL immediately regardless of the numeric score; if any knock-out had fallen below 0.85 confidence, it would have forced NEEDS_REVIEW.
  • Completeness & Merit Point Calculation (30.00 + 61.40 = 91.40 / 100.0 pts): All six +5.0 completeness checks passed cleanly—has_local_partners (p = 0.980), has_validation_plan (p = 0.975), has_quarterly_milestones (p = 0.967), has_qualified_team (p = 0.961), overhead_under_15pct (p = 0.960), and has_itemized_budget (p = 0.954)—earning 30.00 / 30.00 pts. 5. Cross-Use-Case Empirical Benchmarks & Cost Analysis

Aggregating telemetry across all five live CLI executions (uc1_result.json through uc5_result.json) reveals how consistently the 1-Input × N-Criteria architecture performs across Markdown, multi-page PDF, and high-resolution PNG payloads. Figure 9 summarizes end-to-end API latency, shared-input token savings, and per-run cost across all five use cases.


Figure 9: Live benchmark summary across UC1–UC5 showing sub-second API latency (497.4–856.4 ms, avg 732.6 ms), 92.9%–95.0% input token reduction vs. naive sequential N× calls, and $0.001526 total cost across all 83 criteria with strictly 0 output tokens.

Four empirical findings stand out from Figure 9:

  • Consistent Sub-Second Latency Across All Modalities: End-to-end HTTP round-trip latency ranged from 497.37 ms (UC1, 18 criteria on Markdown) to 856.42 ms (UC2, 20 criteria on a multi-page PDF), with an overall average of 732.6 ms across all 5 runs (UC3 = 836.97 ms, UC4 = 702.58 ms, UC5 = 769.60 ms) and 0 retries. Every run completed in a single API batch (batches = 1).
  • 92.9% to 95.0% Input Token Reduction vs. Sequential Calls: Sending the shared document once instead of repeating it once per criterion saved 78 sequential API calls across the 5 workflows (83 total criteria evaluated in 5 calls). Compared with a naive sequential baseline (N × total_input_tokens, analogous to re-sending the entire document once for every single checklist question), shared-input evaluation cut input token volume by 94.4% on UC1 (2,562 vs. 46,116), 95.0% on UC2 (3,809 vs. 76,180), 93.8% on UC3 (2,286 vs. 36,576), 92.9% on UC4 (3,261 vs. 45,654), and 93.3% on UC5 (3,339 vs. 50,085).
  • Strictly Zero Output Tokens Across All 83 Criteria: Across all five runs, total_input_tokens summed to 15,257 tokens, while output_tokens remained strictly 0 ($0.00 output cost).
  • Sub-Cent Total Cost ($0.001526 for All 5 Audits Combined): At $0.10 per 1M input tokens Ref, individual audit costs ranged from $0.000229 (UC3) to $0.000381 (UC2). Evaluating all 83 multimodal criteria across five full documents cost $0.001526 total—roughly 655 full multi-document audit suites per US dollar.

6. Beyond These Five Use Cases: Future Horizons for ZOMA

The five live benchmarks in this article focused on Markdown, PDF, and PNG inputs, yet gemini-decision-1 natively supports a 262,144-token unified multimodal context spanning text, JSON, PDFs, images, audio, and video Ref. Whenever an organization needs to inspect one rich artifact against dozens or hundreds of structured rules, the exact same ZOMA pattern applies without changing the architecture. Figure 10 highlights six additional high-leverage applications across industries.


Figure 10: Six additional real-world applications of Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA) across audio, video, combined image+PDF packets, code diffs, long regulatory PDFs, and autonomous AI agent guardrails.

As illustrated in Figure 10, ZOMA extends naturally well beyond document and ad checks:

  • Customer Support Call & Sales Recording QA (AUDIO): Submit one recorded support or sales call natively as audio against 50+ compliance, script-adherence, empathy, and mandatory legal-disclosure rules (noul + score) in a single pass—with no separate speech-to-text transcription pipeline required.
  • Video Ad, Tutorial & Broadcast Compliance Screening (VIDEO): Evaluate one short promotional clip or training video directly against brand safety, age-rating, logo visibility, caption accuracy, and regulatory claim policies before publication.
  • Insurance Claim & Field Inspection Verification (IMAGE + PDF): Combine damage photos and a contractor estimate PDF into one shared input and audit it against policy coverage knock-outs, fraud indicators, and automated payout tiers using Mode B (weighted_scoring).
  • CI/CD Pull Request & Infrastructure Policy Gate (CODE / DIFF): Screen one pull-request diff, Dockerfile, or Terraform plan against 100+ internal security, privacy, and architectural guidelines in under a second inside CI/CD pipelines or autonomous coding loops.
  • Clinical Trial, ISO & ESG Regulatory Dossier Pre-Audit (LONG PDF 256K): Pre-check lengthy statutory filings—such as medical study protocols, ISO quality manuals, or ESG sustainability disclosures—against hundreds of regulatory clauses before paying for formal external audits.
  • Real-Time AI Agent Safety & Tool-Call Guardrails (JSON / AGENT): Gate proposed actions, tool arguments, or generated deliverables from autonomous agents (such as Antigravity or Claude) against dozens of safety, PII, and policy boundaries in a single sub-second forward pass before execution.

7. Limitations, Best Practices & Summary

While Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA) excels at high-throughput verification and structured scoring, treating it as a drop-in replacement for every generative workflow is a mistake. Five engineering principles keep production deployments reliable:

  • Pair Decisions API with a Reasoning Model When Explanations Are Required: Because gemini-decision-1 emits zero output tokens, it tells you which clauses failed (risk_uncapped_customer_indemnity: p = 0.973) and how confident it is, not how to redline the contract prose. The optimal production pattern is a two-stage cascade: run decisions_audit.py on 100% of incoming documents at ~$0.0003 each, and invoke a generative reasoning model only on the specific FAIL or NEEDS_REVIEW items that require written redlines or student feedback.
  • Embed ZOMA Directly Inside AI Agents (Antigravity, Claude, and Beyond): Because the tool is a stateless Python CLI with --format json output, agentic platforms like Antigravity and Claude can call cli/decisions_audit.py as an external quality gate during autonomous workflows—checking their own generated manuscripts, specs, or images against dozens of organization rules in under a second for roughly $0.0003, then fixing only the flagged FAIL or NEEDS_REVIEW items before handing the final output to a human.
  • Write Atomic, Observable Checklist Criteria: Compound questions ("Does the contract include SOC 2, AES-256, and 72-hour breach notice?") blur probabilities when only two of three clauses are present. Splitting them into atomic noul criteria costs only a few extra question tokens per item while keeping calibrated probabilities sharp.
  • Tune Confidence Thresholds & Borderline Margins to Domain Risk: Defaulting to confidence_threshold = 0.85 works well for general pre-flight checks, as demonstrated by UC1 and UC2 catching ambiguous items automatically. For regulated legal or medical gates, raising the threshold to 0.90–0.95 widens the NEEDS_REVIEW safety band so borderline cases always reach human reviewers.
  • Respect the 1,000-Question Batch Boundary: Each POST /v1beta/decisions request accepts up to 1,000 questions Ref. Our client.py automatically chunks larger checklists into sequential 1,000-question batches while preserving the shared input, though keeping single-document checklists focused and non-redundant maximizes signal clarity.

Summary

Instead of asking an AI chatbot to read a file and write long answers one question at a time, Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA) sends one document, PDF, or image once to Google's Gemini Decisions API (gemini-decision-1) Ref and checks up to 1,000 rules in a single pass—with zero text generated and exact, trustworthy results:

  • Under a Second and Almost Free to Run: Across all five live tests (83 checks across Markdown, PDF, and PNG files), every audit finished in under 1 second (average 732.6 ms), generated 0 output tokens, cut input tokens by 92.9%–95.0% compared to checking rules one by one, and cost $0.001526 in total—roughly 655 full five-document audits for a single US dollar.
  • Catches Real Problems Without Blindly Guessing (Mode A): On technical drafts, vendor contracts, and ad images, ZOMA reliably caught confidentiality leaks, risky legal clauses, and prohibited ad promises—and whenever a rule fell in a gray area, it automatically flagged NEEDS_REVIEW so a human could make the final call.
  • Exact, Math-Error-Free Grading and Screening (Mode B): On student case studies (86.17 / 100) and grant applications (91.40 / 100), the AI evaluates each rubric item while a simple Python script handles all additions, penalties, and mandatory eligibility rules—eliminating AI calculation mistakes completely.
  • Ready for Both Everyday Users and AI Agents: You can immediately run the same tool on your own local files and custom checklists without building OCR or complex code, and autonomous AI agents like Antigravity and Claude can call it directly as a fast, low-cost self-check before delivering finished work.

All scripts, sample documents, checklists, and live test logs are ready to clone and run from tanaikech/gemini-decisions-api-python Ref.

event_model_payload.headline: Auditing Documents & Images with Gemini Decisions API
event_model_payload.summary:
Check any PDF, draft, or image against 1,000 criteria at once—with zero output tokens

Introduction

In my previous article, "Zero-Output-Token AI in Google Apps Script with Gemini Decisions API" Ref (source repository Ref), I demonstrated how Google DeepMind's Gemini Decisions API (POST https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/decisions, powered by gemini-decision-1) Ref fits Google Workspace automation—covering Gmail inbox labeling, model cascade routing, and a Google Sheets PDF compliance audit. Among those examples, the PDF compliance audit drew an especially strong response, and I received inquiries about it from readers across many different fields.

The origin of that idea was actually very personal: before turning it into a Google Sheets demo, I had been using the Decisions API in my own daily writing workflow to check my own research papers, technical articles, manuscripts, and drafts against a self-defined set of review criteria all at once, surfacing issues instantaneously. When developers first encounter a classification endpoint like the Decisions API, the natural mental model is "Many-Inputs × Few-Labels"—classifying a stream of emails or support tickets into three to five categories. Flipping that geometry to "1-Input × up to 1,000-Criteria"—sending one rich multimodal artifact (a PDF, research paper, article manuscript, or ad creative) once and evaluating it against up to 1,000 independent questions in a single forward pass—turned out to be a usage pattern that most users had never envisioned.

Because of that response, I decided to write this dedicated follow-up article focused exclusively on this technique, which I refer to as Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA). Because gemini-decision-1 evaluates all questions against the shared input simultaneously without autoregressive text decoding Ref, ZOMA produces strictly zero output tokens ($0.00 output cost, with input tokens billed once at $0.10 per 1M input tokens) Ref while returning calibrated probabilities (0.01 to 0.99), discrete choices, and ordinal rubric scores (0–4). Moving beyond Google Apps Script into a universal, dependency-light Python 3 CLI published at gemini-decisions-api-python Ref, this article presents a reusable ZOMA auditing and weighted-scoring architecture and validates it across five live multimodal use cases (83 total criteria across Markdown, PDF, and PNG inputs). While I designed the core scenario and evaluation criteria for each of the five use cases myself, the sample input documents used to demonstrate and reproduce each run were generated with Gemini via samples/generate_samples.py Ref so that anyone can reproduce every benchmark without proprietary files; every latency, token count, probability, score, and cost figure reported in this article comes directly from live API runs, and you can immediately swap in your own local files and custom checklists.

In Plain English: What Is ZOMA?

Imagine handing a 20-page vendor contract, a research manuscript draft, an advertising banner, a student essay, or a grant proposal to a meticulous reviewer along with a structured checklist—and receiving every checkbox verdict, every 0–4 quality rating, and a clear flag on any ambiguous clause that needs human judgment back in under one second, for a fraction of a cent. That is Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA). Instead of asking an AI chatbot to write long prose explanations one question at a time, ZOMA sends your document once, evaluates dozens or hundreds of independent checklist rules simultaneously, and lets deterministic Python code handle all final math and pass/fail decisions.

Key Terms in Plain English

  • Single Forward Pass & Zero Output Tokens: Standard AI chatbots generate answers one word (token) at a time, which adds latency and output billing. A single forward pass reads your document once and returns structured numeric answers directly, generating zero written text and zero output-token cost.
  • Calibrated Probability (0.01–0.99): A reliability-tuned percentage expressed from 0.01 (1% likely "Yes") to 0.99 (99% likely "Yes"). When the model is genuinely unsure (for example, 0.72), the score sits in the middle instead of pretending to be 99% certain.
  • Question Types (noul, choice, score): The three structured question formats supported by the Decisions API—noul for Yes/No checks, choice for picking one label from a fixed list, and score for rating quality on an ordered rubric such as 0 to 4.
  • OCR-Free Multimodal Input: Sending PDFs and images (like PNG banners) directly to the AI model as-is, without running a separate Optical Character Recognition (OCR) or PDF-to-text converter first.
  • CLI, JSON/YAML & Dry-Run: A Command-Line Interface (CLI) is a lightweight terminal program; JSON and YAML are plain-text formats used to write your checklist rules; and --dry-run checks your files and rules locally before making any paid API call.
  • Knock-Out Gate: A mandatory eligibility requirement (such as a maximum grant budget cap) where failing that single rule disqualifies a submission immediately, regardless of how high its overall quality score is.

1. Why Gemini Decisions API Excels at ZOMA & Architecture

Low latency and low cost are the most immediately visible advantages of gemini-decision-1, yet its deeper architectural strengths are what make Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA) production-grade across legal, editorial, visual, and academic domains Ref:

  • Sub-Second Single Forward-Pass Latency: Because the model evaluates all questions in a single prefill forward pass (reading the document once without generating text word-by-word) without autoregressive token-by-token decoding, end-to-end latency remains flat and sub-second (497.4–856.4 ms live measured across 14–20 criteria) instead of scaling linearly with output length.
  • Ultra-Low Cost with Strictly Zero Output Tokens: Shared document input tokens are billed once at $0.10 per 1M input tokens Ref, while output and thinking tokens remain strictly 0 ($0.00 output cost), cutting input volume by over 92% compared to sequential per-criterion calls.
  • Mathematically Calibrated Probabilities & Native Confidence Gating: Unlike generative LLMs whose self-reported verbal confidence is often poorly calibrated, gemini-decision-1 returns statistically calibrated probabilities (0.01–0.99) and confidence scores, enabling reliable automated NEEDS_REVIEW escalation thresholds (such as 0.85).
  • Zero JSON Parse Failures & Closed-Set Schema Guarantees: Because no free-form text is decoded into JSON strings, malformed JSON, hallucinated enum values, and schema drift are structurally impossible across noul, choice (2–255 options), and score (2–255 ordered rubric tiers) primitives Ref.
  • High-Density Parallel Batching (Up to 1,000 Independent Questions): A single request evaluates up to 1,000 independent criteria against the exact same shared context without cross-question prompt contamination or attention degradation from massive compound instructions.
  • 262,144-Token Unified Multimodal Context (OCR-Free): A single shared input accepts up to 262,144 tokens (256K) across mixed modalities—text, JSON, PDFs, images, audio, and video Ref—allowing native inspection of multi-page PDFs and high-resolution ad creatives without external OCR or PDF-to-text pipelines.
  • High Reproducibility for Programmatic Control Flow: Without autoregressive sampling drift or variable thinking-token traces, probability outputs remain highly repeatable across runs, making gemini-decision-1 a dependable upstream signal provider for deterministic downstream software logic.

Separation of Concerns

A common problem in LLM-based evaluation pipelines is asking a single generative model to read a document, judge 20 criteria, apply custom business weights, check hard eligibility rules, and sum the final score in one autoregressive JSON response. When AI judgment and arithmetic are mixed together, models exhibit silent summation drift, inconsistent threshold enforcement, and brittle JSON formatting errors.

To prevent these problems by design, our Python CLI enforces a strict two-layer separation of concerns, illustrated in Figure 1.


Figure 1: Shifting from sequential autoregressive LLM loops to 1-Input × up to 1,000-Criteria evaluation with strict separation between gemini-decision-1 inference (client.py) and deterministic Python aggregation (evaluator.py).

As shown in Figure 1, the pipeline divides responsibility across three focused modules:

  • Stateless Multimodal Transport (cli/client.py) Ref: Reads a local .md, .txt, .pdf, .png, .jpg, .jpeg, or .webp file once, Base64-encodes binary documents and images natively without OCR middleware (packaging PDFs and images directly for the API without separate text-extraction tools), authenticates strictly via the x-goog-api-key HTTP header, automatically chunks checklists exceeding 1,000 questions into compliant batches, applies bounded exponential backoff on HTTP 429/5xx, and normalizes proto-JSON response fields into typed Python dictionaries.
  • Zero-Output-Token Semantic Inference (gemini-decision-1): Evaluates every criterion independently against the shared input in one forward pass, returning calibrated noul probabilities (0.01–0.99), choice probability distributions, or score expected values and ordinal bucket distributions—with 0 output tokens generated.
  • Deterministic Evaluation Engine (cli/evaluator.py) Ref: Operates completely offline with zero network I/O. It applies exact threshold rules, risk-flag inversions (expected: "no"), hard knock-out gates, weighted linear scaling, negative penalty deductions, and borderline/low-confidence escalation in pure Python—verified offline by the Stage-3 boundary stress test suite (an automated offline check that verifies the math handles edge cases like zero scores or borderline ties) cli/test_evaluator_stress.py Ref.

This decoupling guarantees that LLM arithmetic hallucination is structurally impossible: the AI model only produces calibrated per-criterion signals, while Python owns every threshold comparison, weighted sum, and pass/fail verdict. Table 1 compares the two deterministic operating modes built into evaluator.py alongside a traditional autoregressive LLM loop.


Table 1: Comparison of Naive Autoregressive LLM Loops vs. Gemini Decisions API Mode A (audit) and Mode B (weighted_scoring) across token scaling, output tokens, arithmetic determinism, and human-in-the-loop gating.

Table 1 highlights why a single checklist schema can drive two distinct enterprise patterns:

  • Mode A (audit): Designed for binary compliance, pre-flight linting, and risk scanning. Each noul criterion specifies expected: "yes" (required safeguard) or expected: "no" (prohibited risk flag). Any signal whose confidence falls below confidence_threshold (default 0.85, i.e., 0.15 < P < 0.85) is routed automatically to NEEDS_REVIEW rather than guessed. For choice criteria, explicit fail_choices or review_choices trigger FAIL or NEEDS_REVIEW; for score criteria, expected scores are gated against pass_min and fail_max.
  • Mode B (weighted_scoring): Designed for rubric grading, grant screening, and procurement scoring. Criteria can be marked as knockout: true (hard eligibility gates where a FAIL immediately disqualifies the submission regardless of points, and low confidence forces NEEDS_REVIEW), positive-weight noul or score dimensions (where an ordinal 0–4 score contributes (score / max_scale) * weight points), or negative-weight noul penalty flags. How to read the live numbers in Sections 3 and 4:

  • Required checks (expected: "yes"): We want the document to contain this element, so a high probability (p >= 0.85) means PASS, while a very low probability (p <= 0.15) means FAIL (missing requirement).
  • Risk & defect flags (expected: "no"): We want this problem to be absent, so a low probability (p <= 0.15) means PASS (safe), while a high probability (p >= 0.85) means FAIL (risk or violation detected).
  • Human-review zone (0.15 < P < 0.85): Whenever the model's confidence is below 0.85, the tool refuses to guess and routes that criterion to NEEDS_REVIEW for a human reviewer.
  • Rubric scores (0–4, e.g., 3.17 / 4): Rather than forcing a blunt whole number, the model returns a probability distribution across levels 0 through 4 and computes the weighted average (expected score) for fine-grained grading.

  • Customer Support Call & Sales Recording QA (AUDIO): Submit one recorded support or sales call natively as audio against 50+ compliance, script-adherence, empathy, and mandatory legal-disclosure rules (noul + score) in a single pass—with no separate speech-to-text transcription pipeline required.

7. Limitations, Best Practices & Summary

While Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA) excels at high-throughput verification and structured scoring, treating it as a drop-in replacement for every generative workflow is a mistake. Five engineering principles keep production deployments reliable:

  • Pair Decisions API with a Reasoning Model When Explanations Are Required: Because gemini-decision-1 emits zero output tokens, it tells you which clauses failed (risk_uncapped_customer_indemnity: p = 0.973) and how confident it is, not how to redline the contract prose.   • Tune Confidence Thresholds & Borderline Margins to Domain Risk: Defaulting to confidence_threshold = 0.85 works well for general pre-flight checks, as demonstrated by UC1 and UC2 catching ambiguous items automatically. Instead of asking an AI chatbot to read a file and write long answers one question at a time, Zero-Output Multimodal Auditing (ZOMA) sends one document, PDF, or image once to Google's Gemini Decisions API (gemini-decision-1) Ref and checks up to 1,000 rules in a single pass—with zero text generated and exact, trustworthy results:

  • Ready for Both Everyday Users and AI Agents: You can immediately run the same tool on your own local files and custom checklists without building OCR or complex code, and autonomous AI agents like Antigravity and Claude can call it directly as a fast, low-cost self-check before delivering finished work.

title: FastAPI: polling fiable para emails de prueba
summary:
Cuando una prueba de registro necesita leer un email, el problema rara vez es hacer una petición HTTP. Lo dificil es decidir cuánto esperar, qué hacer con una respuesta vacía y cómo distinguir un fallo temporal de un error definitivo. Un pequeño contrato de polling hace que una suite de FastAPI sea más estable y que sus logs expliquen mejor lo ocurrido.

En este artículo propongo un patrón simple para consultar una bandeja de pruebas, como un flujo basado en tempmail.so o tempmailso, sin acoplar la prueba a un proveedor concreto. La idea sirve igual para un inbox local, un mock o un servicio externo.

Por qué un polling ingenuo se vuelve frágil

El primer intento suele ser un while True con un sleep(1). Funciona en el portátil, pero en CI aparecen tres problemas:

  • El test puede esperar para siempre si el mensaje nunca llega.
  • Varias ejecuciones pueden leer el mismo mensaje y pisarse.
  • Un intervalo fijo genera carga innecesaria cuando el proveedor está lento.

También es común confundir “no hay mensaje todavía” con “la API falló”. Son estados distintos. Un 404 de una consulta por mensaje puede ser una respuesta esperable, mientras que un 401 necesita detener la prueba de inmediato.

Para entender el flujo completo, ayuda revisar esta evidencia útil para validar emails. El punto clave es conservar señales suficientes para depurar sin guardar el contenido privado del correo.

El contrato mínimo de un poller

Antes de escribir el cliente, definamos el resultado. Un poller útil debería devolver exactamente uno de estos estados:

  1. received: llegó un mensaje que coincide con la correlación de la prueba.
  2. timeout: se agotó el tiempo total sin recibirlo.
  3. failed: la API respondió con un error no recuperable.

El tiempo total debe ser un límite, no una recomendación. Además, cada consulta necesita un identificador único, por ejemplo un alias de inbox por ejecución y un asunto que incluya un nonce. Así la Automatización no recoge un mensaje viejo por accidente.

Una implementación pequeña con FastAPI

El siguiente cliente separa la consulta del reloj y del criterio de coincidencia. Es pequeño, pero tiene las decisiones importantes: deadline monotónico, backoff limitado y un error explícito.

import asyncio
import time
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Message:
    message_id: str
    subject: str


class PollTimeout(Exception):
    pass


async def wait_for_message(
    fetch: Callable[[], Awaitable[list[Message]]],
    matches: Callable[[Message], bool],
    timeout_seconds: float = 30.0,
) -> Message:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout_seconds
    delay = 0.5

    while True:
        for message in await fetch():
            if matches(message):
                return message

        remaining = deadline - time.monotonic()
        if remaining <= 0:
            raise PollTimeout("No llegó el email dentro del límite")

        await asyncio.sleep(min(delay, remaining))
        delay = min(delay * 1.7, 5.0)

En una ruta de FastAPI, el endpoint que crea la prueba puede devolver un test_id y el alias asociado. El worker o el test runner usa ese identificador para consultar mensajes. No conviene que el endpoint espere la llegada del email: mantiene ocupado un recurso y hace más dificil controlar cancelaciones.

El criterio matches también debe comprobar el destinatario, el asunto y, si existe, un token de correlación. No basta con buscar “Verify”, porque dos pruebas paralelas podrian recibir mensajes parecidos.

Cómo hacerlo seguro para Automatización

Hay cuatro prácticas que suelen pagar dividendos:

Usa un inbox por ejecución

Si el proveedor lo permite, crea una dirección o buzón aislado para cada build. En caso contrario, guarda un nonce en la base de datos y exige que aparezca en el asunto. Este aislamiento reduce carreras y vuelve reproducible el fallo.

Haz el consumo idempotente

Después de encontrar un mensaje, registra message_id junto con test_id. Si el runner reintenta por un corte de red, no debería procesar el mismo token dos veces. Una clave única en PostgreSQL es más confiable que un booleano en memoria.

Clasifica los errores

Reintenta límites de tasa, timeouts de red y respuestas 5xx con backoff. Detén el flujo ante 4xx de autenticación o una respuesta con un esquema inválido. Los logs tambien deben incluir el intento y el tiempo restante, nunca el token completo ni el cuerpo del email.

Prueba el reloj, no el tiempo real

En los tests unitarios, inyecta un reloj o sustituye fetch por una secuencia controlada: vacío, vacío y mensaje. Prueba también el caso en que el mensaje llega justo después del deadline. Es un detalle pequeño que evita pruebas intermitentes.

Para separar mejor los datos temporales por entorno, puedes combinar este patrón con aislar pruebas de correo por entorno. Parece obvio, pero muchos pipelines mezclan fixtures de staging y CI por que comparten una cuenta.

Checklist de pruebas

Antes de dar por terminado el cliente, revisa:

  • ¿Existe un timeout total configurable?
  • ¿El intervalo está limitado y usa backoff?
  • ¿El mensaje se correlaciona con la ejecución actual?
  • ¿Un reintento es idempotente?
  • ¿Se diferencian timeout, error transitorio y error permanente?
  • ¿Los logs omiten secretos y contenido sensible?
  • ¿Se limpia el fixture al finalizar, incluso si la prueba falla?

Si buscas ejemplos de herramientas, quizá escribas temp org mail al explorar opciones. Para el código, sin embargo, conviene mantener una interfaz propia y tratar el proveedor como un adaptador reemplazable.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Qué timeout debería usar?

Empieza con el p95 observado en CI y añade margen para una cola lenta. No copies un número fijo sin medir: el entorno local y el runner compartido se comportan distinto.

¿Es mejor hacer polling o usar webhooks?

Un webhook reduce consultas cuando el proveedor es confiable, pero añade una ruta pública, firma y manejo de reintentos. Polling con deadline suele ser más practico para una suite pequeña. Se puede migrar después si el volumen lo justifica.

¿Debo guardar el email completo para depurar?

Normalmente no. Guarda el message_id, timestamps, estado y una razón resumida. Si necesitas el cuerpo, redáctalo y limita su retención; un fixture de prueba no merece convertirse en un archivo permanente.

El resultado buscado no es que cada email llegue instantaneamente. Es que, cuando llegue tarde o no llegue, FastAPI y la prueba puedan decir qué pasó, cuánto esperaron y qué acción corresponde.
